For COVID he took on what many saw as a conspiracy theory . <p> In the dawning days of the new millennium , Michael Worobey staggered out of the Congolese jungle with a cooler full of chimpanzee poop . <p> Within the first few hours of the expedition , Worobey had impaled his hand on a barbed plant . Unbeknownst to him , the thorn was still lodged deep in his flesh . As Worobey and two other scientists combed the forest for the specimens , his wound began to fester . <p> His hand turned black , and he spiked a high fever . Discolouration began streaking up his arm . <p> " I wanted to stay until we had some chimp s--t samples to take back to town , " he says . <p> By the time he left the jungle , Worobey , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ suffering a life-threatening infection . He got treatment and lived . But the senior scientist leading the trip , a pre-eminent evolutionary biologist named Bill Hamilton , was stricken with malaria and died weeks later . <p> When the cooler full of chimpanzee excrement finally reached Oxford , two vials of urine held the clues to the mystery they had been seeking to solve : the source of pandemic HIV . <p> Worobey , a Canadian from Salmon Arm , B.C. , has devoted his career to tracking the origin of important viruses , especially pandemic ones . He is known both for his meticulousness in teasing secrets out of viral genes , and for his willingness to get his hands dirty -- even gangrenous -- in the search for evidence beyond the lab . <p> Worobey 's job has sometimes thrust him into the white-hot centre of controversy . His work has been attacked by ambassadors , by rappers , and by other scientists . <p> In the hunt for the origins of the current pandemic , amid geopolitical jockeying and online vitriol , Worobey has followed a trail @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> In May 2021 , he signed his name to a letter in the prestigious journal Science that urged researchers to seriously investigate whether the virus that causes COVID was accidentally released from a lab . The letter gave the lab-leak theory a major credibility boost and helped launch it into the mainstream ; less than two weeks later , U.S. President Joe Biden announced a 90-day intelligence review of the pandemic 's origins . <p> But in the two years since the letter was published , Worobey 's own research has produced some of the most compelling evidence yet that the virus spilled over from wild animals . Among the possible culprits : the previously obscure raccoon dog . <p> Discovering the origin of a virus , especially a pandemic one , is always more than an academic exercise . <p> Some of history 's most lethal pathogens have been controlled by following the path of infection back to its source : a flea-infested colony of rats , for the Black Plague , or a contaminated water pump on London 's Broad Street , in the case of cholera @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ investigations are always embedded in the same societies just decimated by an invisible reaper . Competing viral origin stories absorb the miasma of fear , anger and guilt left in the plague 's wake , making it even harder to tease out the truth . <p> The COVID origins debate is often framed as a geopolitical battle : China vs . U.S.A. , Republicans vs . Democrats . Between politicians rambling bout nucleotides , epidemiologists blaming dark conspiracies , and how every fact gets refracted in the funhouse mirror that is Twitter , it can be hard to tell which theory has the upper hand . Some people say we will likely never know the truth . <p> Worobey does n't say that . <p> " When we look at the big picture of all of the evidence , " he says , " it 's like a bright red arrow flashing : ' This is where it started . ' " <h> New ways to unlock viruses ' secrets <p> Worobey , 50 , who heads the University of Arizona 's ecology and evolutionary biology department , often uses @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are always throwing off sparks . If a spark hits a rock or water , it dies . But if a spark hits a patch of dry grass , it can quickly spread out of control . <p> He would know : as a university student , Worobey spent his summers working for the B.C. Wildfire Service 's Rapattack crew , an elite team of firefighters based out of Salmon Arm , his hometown in the province 's interior . Members of the Rapattack team are trained to rappel from helicopters and battle hard-to-access blazes . <p> Aside from being " absolutely the best " college job ever , he says , Worobey 's experience with the Wildfire Service offered an unexpected boost into some of the most cutting-edge virus research of the era . <p> As an undergraduate student at Simon Fraser University , Worobey applied for the Rhodes Scholarship , an international program that brings students to study at Oxford . The scholarship is famously selective , and beyond high grades , screens for candidates who excel in sports or the arts , especially in team settings . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , he remembers . He got in . <p> When he arrived at Oxford in 1997 , Worobey joined the zoology department , but was n't sure what specifically he would focus on . A virologist and evolutionary biologist named Eddie Holmes asked if he wanted to study dengue , an emerging virus transmitted by mosquitoes . <p> " Mike came in as this very quiet , kind of mild-mannered , gentle , quite unassuming PhD student from Canada , who was very hard-working and had a quiet determination to get things done , " says Holmes . <p> " Next thing you know he 's off in the Congo with Bill Hamilton sampling chimpanzees to find the origin of HIV , " he says . " You look back in hindsight and think , ' My God . That was bloody mad . ' " <p> Holmes and a small group of colleagues in the department were pioneering ways to force viruses to spill their inner secrets . Computers , genetic sequencing and other molecular tools had all recently become much more powerful . With a flood of genetic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ do it with , scientists were inventing powerful methods of probing viral family trees . <p> Viruses pick up mutations as they pass from cell to cell . Comparing how similar or different viruses ' genome sequences are to each other determines their spot on the family tree , bunching viruses together that are more like sisters and brothers , branching off other groups that are distant cousins , and pinpointing what the ancestor of them all probably looked like , and when it existed . <p> One of the biggest breakthroughs was applying a " molecular clock " to a family tree . All viruses evolve at different rates . With enough viral samples collected at different time points , the researchers could figure out how many mutations accumulate each month , or year , and then calculate how long ago their most recent common ancestor existed . This can be used to estimate the time the first infection appeared in a region , or even in the world . <p> " When you put a bunch of these genome sequences together and sort of trace those mutations back @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the source of things , it just opened up so much more information about how really important pathogens get into humans and then spread , " says Worobey . <p> " It was exciting to have the ability to use the information in the viruses themselves against them . " <p> Worobey had been working with these techniques for a couple years when Hamilton , the famous evolutionary biologist , invited him on an expedition to probe a theory about the origins of HIV . <p> Not just any theory : the January 2000 trip was a quest to investigate the hypothesis that HIV emerged from , essentially , a botched science experiment . <p> Unlike Hamilton , Worobey thought the theory was unlikely . But no hypothesis can be refuted without evidence , and Worobey still says the evidence was worth the struggle to get it . " <h> How did AIDS spread across the world ? <p> In the 1950s , a Polish-American researcher named Hilary Koprowski was among the scientists racing to invent the first polio vaccine . Koprowski created an oral vaccine that relied on a weakened version of the virus grown in live cells . He conducted trials for his vaccine in what was then the colonial Belgian Congo and other nearby countries , administering it in nearly a quarter-million people . <p> Four decades later after Koprowski 's trial , a troubling theory took hold . <p> By 2000 , AIDS , HIV 's brutal and chameleonic syndrome , had been recognized for almost 20 years . But crucial questions about the virus remained unanswered : How , where and when did it first infect people ? And how did it spread across the world ? <p> Scientists had discovered many related viruses in captive and wild African primates , and called these monkey pathogens simian immunodeficiency virus ( SIV ) . The trial then transmitted the virus directly into people via a contaminated vaccine , the theory held . <p> Very few researchers working directly on HIV believed this , and Koprowski denied this was how his vaccine was made . But media stories and a popular book inflated the theory 's visibility . @@98499872 <h> If Trudeau is still interested in ' real change , ' Liberal supporters have some ideas <p> It seems fair to assume that Justin Trudeau 's days of representing political change are long past . ( Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press ) <p> When Prime Minister Justin Trudeau takes the stage and addresses Liberals at their biennial convention next week , he will have been leader of the party for a decade and prime minister for seven and a half years . <p> So it seems fair to assume that his days of representing political change are long past . " Real change " was the right slogan for 2015 , but it 's 2023 now . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the reformist spirit that marked his early years as Liberal leader , party members have some ideas . <p> So far , Trudeau 's record as a political reformer has been both loudly underwhelming and quietly consequential . <p> His signature commitment to electoral reform -- he famously vowed that the 2015 election would be the last federal vote conducted under the first-past-the-post system -- collapsed in a heap after a convoluted consultation . The promise of a new era of government transparency amounted to only minor changes . And an attempt at comprehensive parliamentary reform was largely abandoned after an opposition filibuster . <p> It stands to reason that the most dramatic changes of a prime minister 's tenure are most likely to happen in the early days -- when the government is fresh and new and most eager to mark a break from its predecessor , before the burdens of governing crowd out all other concerns . <p> At this stage , the Trudeau government 's chances of re-election also seem to depend most on the basic business of governing -- implementing policy , fulfilling the numerous commitments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and building out a record to run on . <p> But of the 36 policy resolutions set to be debated by Liberals in Ottawa next week , the most interesting are four proposals for political and democratic reform -- a citizen 's assembly on electoral reform , mandatory voting , a " **30;84;TOOLONG " law and a lower voting age . <p> All such proposals come with a significant caveat : the party leader and the government are not required to heed the resolutions passed at party conventions . Ultimately , it 's the senior Liberal leadership that writes the party 's election platforms and the government 's budgets . <h> The pros and cons of reform <p> The first of those four reform proposals would require Trudeau to revisit the scene of his failed promise on electoral reform . However awkward it might be , doing so might give him a chance to atone for his original sin . <p> The case for making voting mandatory -- as it is in Australia -- rests on the belief that voter turnout is n't as high as it should be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the most recent Australian election was 90 per cent . But there remains the question of whether making voting mandatory would actually improve citizen engagement or the relative quality of Canadian democracy -- beyond simply increasing the absolute number of people voting . <p> Students line up at a polling station at Ryerson University in Toronto during the 2015 election . ( Marta Iwanek/The Canadian Press ) <p> When the special committee on electoral reform considered mandatory voting in 2016 , it also noted a " general discomfort " with the notion of " penalizing people for not participating in the electoral process . " <p> A " truth-in-advertising " law for political ads holds a certain immediate appeal . Most people like the truth . And many people think politicians do n't always tell the simple truth . But writing a suitable law would be easier said than done and it 's hard to guess at how effective it would even be -- politicians generally do n't lie so much as they as are selective about facts and context . <p> Changing the voting age is by no means @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Reid Institute found that just 25 per cent of survey respondents supported lowering the voting age to 16 ; even among those between the ages of 18 and 34 , support was only 34 per cent . Mandatory voting , meanwhile , was supported by 52 per cent . And Trudeau himself voted against an NDP MP 's bill last fall that would have lowered the voting age . <p> But Trudeau has long associated himself with the causes of young people . He chaired a task force on engaging young Canadians as part of a Liberal Party renewal process in 2006 , then promoted the idea of a national youth service program after he got elected in 2008 . When he became prime minister in 2015 , he made himself minister of youth and appointed an official youth council to advise him ( members of the council can be as young as 16 ) . <h> A compromise approach to the voting age <p> When speaking before an audience of young people , Trudeau invariably tells them that they should think of themselves not just as " leaders of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it 's young people who have the most to gain or lose from the dominant public policy issue of the moment and one of the Trudeau government 's most loudly stated policy priorities : climate change . <p> While Trudeau and the cabinet voted against the bill to lower the voting age in the fall , 20 Liberal MPs voted in favour ( they were joined by every NDP and Bloc Quebecois MP ) . The resolution prepared for the upcoming Liberal convention also offers a compromise . Noting that previous calls to lower the voting age to 16 have failed , the resolution sponsored by the Alberta wing of the party suggests moving the voting age to 17 . <p> Maybe that extra year makes a difference to Liberals . It would at least give them cover to move now after rejecting the NDP bill last fall . <p> The courts might eventually force Parliament 's hand -- a legal challenge filed in 2021 will test the Supreme Court 's suggestion in 2019 that any limit on the right to vote needs to have a " compelling justification . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in countries like Scotland and New Zealand at least make the case that lowering the voting age in Canada is an idea worth serious consideration -- something more than the usual scoffing about " kids these days . " <p> Then again , Liberals might simply decide that rejecting this motion would be too ironic . After all , their party constitution allows registered Liberals as young as 14 to vote at conventions . <h> ABOUT THE AUTHOR <p> Aaron Wherry has covered Parliament Hill since 2007 and has written for Maclean 's , the National Post and the Globe and Mail . Temperatures this year were already hitting the high 90s the first week of April . <p> A WARMING WORLD <p> " Phoenix really is the model for what we 'll be seeing in other places , " said researcher Jennifer Ailshire , a native of the desert city now at the University of Southern California 's Leonard Davis School of Gerontology where she studies how environmental factors affect health and aging . " The world is changing rapidly and I fear we are not acting fast enough to teach people how harmful rising temperatures can be . " <p> A 2021 study estimated more than a third of U.S. heat deaths each year can be attributed to human-caused global warming . @@98500493 <h> Wildfires in Anchorage ? Climate change sparks disaster fears <p> Flames are visible from the Beluga Point parking area near Anchorage , Alaska , on July 19 , 2016 , as a wildfire near McHugh Creek burns . A recent series of wildfires near Anchorage and the hottest day on record have sparked fears that a warming climate could soon mean serious , untenable blazes in urban areas -- just like in the rest of the drought-plagued American West . ( Marc Lester/Anchorage Daily News via AP ) <p> This is the new reality in Alaska 's largest city , where a recent series of wildfires near Anchorage and the hottest day on record have sparked fears that a warming climate could soon mean serious , untenable blazes in urban areas -- just like in the rest of the drought-plagued American West . <p> The risk is particularly high in the city 's burgeoning Anchorage Hillside neighborhood , where multi-million dollar homes have pushed further and further up steep slopes and to the forest 's edge . But as Anchorage has grown , the available land is higher up , where wild and urban areas intersect , and those fires are very different from what his firefighters are trained to combat . <p> The city also has limited wildfire equipment , and it 's nearly impossible to get a fire engine up some switchback roads to homes nestled high up mountains . <p> " Our strategy is basically to put as many resources as we have on duty on a small fire so that we can keep it contained " while waiting for assistance from the Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection , Schrage said . <p> This spring , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ using water hoses to create a line around the perimeter of a fire and the city is encouraging homeowners to participate in a program to identify hazards like brush and old trees that would feed a fire before it 's too late . Half of those fire seasons have occurred since 2002 , including the worst year on record -- 2004 -- when over 10,156 square miles ( 26,304 square kilometers ) burned . <p> From his home high above Anchorage in 2019 , Moore @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in a heavily wooded area of the city .
